{{Short description|Probability distribution}}
A '''ratio distribution''' (also known as a '''quotient distribution''') is a [[probability distribution]] constructed as the distribution of the [[ratio]] (or [[quotient]]) of [[random variable]]s having two other known distributions.
Given two (usually [[statistically independent|independent]]) random variables {{mvar|X}} and {{mvar|Y}}, the distribution of the random variable {{mvar|Z}} that is formed as the ratio {{math|1= ''Z'' = ''X''/''Y''}} is a ''ratio distribution''.

An example is the [[Cauchy distribution]] (also called the ''normal ratio distribution''), which comes about as the ratio of two [[normal distribution|normally distributed]] variables with zero mean.
Two other distributions often used in test-statistics are also ratio distributions:
the {{Student's t-distribution|link=yes}} arises from a [[Gaussian distribution|Gaussian]] random variable divided by an independent [[chi distribution|chi-distributed]] random variable,
while the [[F-distribution|''F''-distribution]] originates from the ratio of two independent [[chi-squared distribution|chi-squared distributed]] random variables.
More general ratio distributions have been considered in the literature.{{sfnp|Geary|1930}}{{sfnp|Curtiss|1941}}{{sfnp|Hinkley|1969}}{{sfnp|Hayya|Armstrong|Gressis|1975}}{{sfnp|Springer|1979}}{{sfnp|Pham-Gia|Turkkan|Marchand|2006}}<ref>{{harvp|Fieller|1932}}; {{harvp|Marsaglia|1964}}; {{harvp|Marsaglia|1965}}.</ref>

Often the ratio distributions are [[heavy-tailed]], and it may be difficult to work with such distributions and develop an associated [[statistical test]].
A method based on the [[median]] has been suggested as a "work-around".{{sfnp|Brody|Williams|Wold|Quake|2002}}

==Algebra of random variables==
{{main|Algebra of random variables}}
The ratio is one type of algebra for random variables:
Related to the ratio distribution are the [[product distribution]], [[sum distribution]] and [[difference distribution]]. More generally, one may talk of combinations of sums, differences, products and ratios.
Many of these distributions are described in [[Melvin D. Springer]]'s book from 1979 ''The Algebra of Random Variables''.{{sfnp|Springer|1979}}

The algebraic rules known with ordinary numbers do not apply for the [[algebra of random variables]].
For example, if a product is {{tmath|1= C=AB}} and a ratio is {{tmath|1= D=C/A}} it does not necessarily mean that the distributions of {{tmath|D}} and {{tmath|B}} are the same.
Indeed, a peculiar effect is seen for the [[Cauchy distribution]]: The product and the ratio of two independent Cauchy distributions (with the same scale parameter and the [[location parameter]] set to zero) will give the same distribution.{{sfnp|Springer|1979}}
This becomes evident when regarding the Cauchy distribution as itself a ratio distribution of two Gaussian distributions of zero means: Consider two Cauchy random variables, {{tmath|C_1}} and {{tmath|C_2}}, each constructed from two Gaussian distributions {{tmath|1= C_1=G_1/G_2}} and {{tmath|1= C_2 = G_3/G_4}}. Then
<math display="block">\frac{C_1}{C_2} = \frac{{G_1}/{G_2}}{{G_3}/{G_4}} = \frac{G_1 G_4}{G_2 G_3} = \frac{G_1}{G_2} \times \frac{G_4}{G_3} = C_1 \times C_3,</math>
where {{tmath|1= C_3 = G_4/G_3}}. The first term is the ratio of two Cauchy distributions while the last term is the product of two such distributions.

==Derivation==
A way of deriving the ratio distribution of {{tmath|1= Z=X/Y}} from the [[Joint probability distribution|joint distribution]] of the two other random variables {{tmath|X}}, {{tmath|Y}}, with joint {{abbr|PDF|probability density function}} {{tmath|p_{X,Y}(x,y)}}, is by integration of the following form{{sfnp|Curtiss|1941}}
<math display="block">p_Z(z) = \int^{+\infty}_{-\infty} |y|\, p_{X,Y}(zy, y) \, dy. </math>

If the two variables are independent then  <math>p_{XY}(x,y) = p_X(x) p_Y(y)</math> and this becomes
<math display="block">p_Z(z) = \int^{+\infty}_{-\infty} |y|\, p_X(zy) p_Y(y) \, dy. </math>

This may not be straightforward. By way of example take the classical problem of the ratio of two standard Gaussian samples. The joint {{abbr|PDF|probability density function}} is
<math display="block"> p_{X,Y}(x,y) = \frac {1}{2 \pi }\exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{2} \right) \exp \left(-\frac{y^2}{2} \right). </math>

Defining <math> Z = X/Y </math> we have
<math display="block"> \begin{align}
p_Z(z) &=  \frac {1}{2 \pi }\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \, |y| \, \exp\left(-\frac{\left(zy\right)^2}{2} \right) \, \exp\left(-\frac{  y^2}{2} \right) \, dy \\
&= \frac {1}{2 \pi } \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}  \,|y| \, \exp\left(-\frac{y^2 \left(z^2 + 1\right)}{2} \right) \, dy.
\end{align} </math>
Using the known [[Integral|definite integral]]  <math display="inline"> \int_0^{\infty} x \exp\left(-cx^2  \right) dx = \frac {1}{2c}</math>  we get
<math display="block">p_Z(z) = \frac {1}{\pi (z^2 + 1)},</math>
which is the Cauchy distribution, or {{Student's t-distribution|link=y}} with {{tmath|1= n = 1}}.

The [[Mellin transform]] has also been suggested for derivation of ratio distributions.{{sfnp|Springer|1979}}

In the case of positive independent variables, proceed as follows. The diagram shows a separable bivariate distribution <math> f_{x,y}(x,y)=f_x(x)f_y(y) </math> which has support in the positive quadrant <math> x,y > 0 </math> and we wish to find the pdf of the ratio {{tmath|1= R= X/Y}}. The hatched volume above the line {{tmath|1= y=x/R}} represents the cumulative distribution of the function {{tmath|f_{x,y}(x,y)}} multiplied with the logical function {{tmath|X/Y\le R}}. The density is first integrated in horizontal strips; the horizontal strip at height {{tmath|y}} extends from {{tmath|1= x=0}} to {{tmath|1= x=Ry}} and has incremental probability <math display="inline">f_y(y)dy \int_0^{Ry} f_x(x)dx</math>.

Secondly, integrating the horizontal strips upward over all {{tmath|y}} yields the volume of probability above the line
<math display="block">F_R(R) = \int_0^\infty f_y(y) \left(\int_0^{Ry} f_x(x)dx \right) dy</math>
Finally, differentiate <math>F_R(R)</math> with respect to <math>R</math> to get the {{abbr|PDF|probability density function}} {{tmath|f_R(R)}}.
<math display="block">f_R(R) = \frac{d}{dR} \left[ \int_0^\infty f_y(y) \left(\int_0^{Ry} f_x(x)dx \right) dy \right]</math>
Move the differentiation inside the integral:
<math display="block">f_R(R) = \int_0^\infty f_y(y) \left(\frac{d}{dR} \int_0^{Ry} f_x(x)dx \right) dy</math>
and since
<math display="block">  \frac{d}{dR} \int_0^{Ry} f_x(x)dx  = yf_x(Ry)</math>
then
<math display="block">f_R(R) = \int_0^\infty f_y(y) f_x(Ry) y dy.  </math>
As an example, find the {{abbr|PDF|probability density function}} of the ratio {{tmath|R}} when
<math display="block">\begin{align}
f_x(x) &= \alpha e^{-\alpha x}, \\
f_y(y) &= \beta e^{-\beta y}, \\
x,y &\ge 0.
\end{align}</math>
[[File:RatioDistribution.jpg|thumb|Evaluating the cumulative distribution of a ratio]]
We have
<math display="block">  \int_0^{Ry} f_x(x)dx = - \left.e^{-\alpha x} \right\vert_0^{Ry} =  1- e^{-\alpha Ry}</math>
thus
<math display="block"> \begin{align} F_R(R) &= \int_0^\infty f_y(y) \left( 1- e^{-\alpha Ry} \right) dy \\
&=\int_0^\infty \beta e^{-\beta y} \left( 1- e^{-\alpha Ry} \right) dy \\
& = 1 - \frac{\alpha R}{\beta + \alpha R} \\
& = \frac{ R}{\tfrac{\beta}{\alpha} +  R}.
\end{align}
</math>
Differentiation with respect to {{tmath|R}} yields the {{abbr|PDF|probability density function}} of {{tmath|R}}:
<math display="block">f_R(R) =\frac{d}{dR} \left(\frac{ R}{\tfrac{\beta}{\alpha} + R}\right) = \frac{\tfrac{\beta}{\alpha}}{\left(\tfrac{\beta}{\alpha} + R \right)^2}.</math>

==Moments of random ratios==

From [[Mellin transform]] theory, for distributions existing only on the positive half-line {{tmath|x \ge 0}}, we have the product identity
<math display="block">\operatorname{E}[(UV)^p] = \operatorname{E}[U^p ] \cdot \operatorname{E}[V^p]</math>
provided {{tmath|U}}, {{tmath|V}} are independent. For the case of a ratio of samples like {{tmath|\operatorname{E}[(X/Y)^p]}}, in order to make use of this identity it is necessary to use moments of the inverse distribution. Set <math>1/Y = Z</math> such that {{tmath|1= \operatorname{E}[(XZ)^p] = \operatorname{E}[X^p] \cdot \operatorname{E}[Y^{-p}] }}.
Thus, if the moments of <math> X^p </math> and <math> Y^{-p}</math> can be determined separately, then the moments of <math> X/Y </math> can be found. The moments of <math> Y^{-p} </math> are determined from the inverse {{abbr|PDF|probability density function}} of {{tmath|Y}}, often a tractable exercise. At simplest, {{tmath|1= \textstyle \operatorname{E}[Y^{-p}] = \int_0^\infty y^{-p} f_y(y)dy }}.

To illustrate, let <math>X</math> be sampled from a standard [[Gamma distribution]]
<math display="block">x^{\alpha - 1}e^{-x}/\Gamma(\alpha) </math> whose {{tmath|p}}-th moment is {{tmath| \Gamma(\alpha + p) / \Gamma(\alpha)}}.

<math>Z = Y^{-1} </math> is sampled from an [[Inverse-gamma distribution|inverse Gamma distribution]] with parameter <math>\beta</math> and has {{abbr|PDF|probability density function}} {{tmath| \Gamma^{-1}(\beta) z^{-(1+\beta)} e^{-1/z} }}. The moments of this PDF are
<math display="block"> \operatorname{E}[Z^p]= \operatorname{E}[Y^{-p}] = \frac { \Gamma(\beta - p)}{ \Gamma(\beta) }, \; p<\beta. </math>

Multiplying the corresponding moments gives
<math display="block"> \operatorname{E}[(X/Y)^p]=\operatorname{E}[X^p] \cdot \operatorname{E}[Y^{-p}] = \frac { \Gamma(\alpha + p)}{ \Gamma(\alpha) } \frac { \Gamma(\beta - p)}{ \Gamma(\beta) }, \; p<\beta. </math>

Independently, it is known that the ratio of the two Gamma samples <math>R = X/Y</math> follows the [[beta prime distribution]]:
<math display="block"> f_{\beta'}(r, \alpha, \beta) = \Beta(\alpha, \beta)^{-1} r^{\alpha-1} (1+r)^{-(\alpha + \beta)} </math>
whose moments are
<math display="block">\operatorname{E}[R^p]= \frac { \Beta(\alpha + p,\beta-p)}{ \Beta(\alpha, \beta)}.</math>

Substituting <math display="inline"> \Beta(\alpha, \beta) =\frac { \Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)}{  \Gamma(\alpha +\beta) } </math>  we have
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\operatorname{E}[R^p] &= \left.\frac {\Gamma(\alpha + p)\Gamma(\beta - p)}{\Gamma(\alpha +\beta)} \right/ \frac{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)}{\Gamma(\alpha +\beta)} \\[.5em]
  &= \frac{\Gamma(\alpha +p)\Gamma(\beta - p)}{\Gamma(\alpha) \Gamma(\beta) },
\end{align}</math>
which is consistent with the product of moments above.

==Means and variances of random ratios==
In the [[Product distribution]] section, and derived from [[Mellin transform]] theory (see section above), it is found that the mean of a product of independent variables is equal to the product of their means.  In the case of ratios, we have
<math display="block"> \operatorname{E}(X/Y) = \operatorname{E}(X) \cdot \operatorname{E}(1/Y) </math>
which, in terms of probability distributions, is equivalent to
<math display="block"> \operatorname{E}(X/Y) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x f_x(x) \, dx  \times \int_{-\infty}^\infty y^{-1} f_y(y) \, dy.</math>

Note that {{tmath|1= \textstyle \operatorname{E}(1/Y) \neq \frac{1}{\operatorname{E}(Y)} }}; i.e., {{tmath|1= \textstyle \int_{-\infty}^\infty y^{-1} f_y(y) \, dy \ne 1\left/\int_{-\infty}^\infty y f_y(y) \, dy\right.}}.

The variance of a ratio of independent variables is
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\operatorname{Var}(X/Y) &= \operatorname{E}([X/Y]^2) - \operatorname{E^2}(X/Y) \\
  &= \operatorname{E}(X^2) \cdot \operatorname{E}(1/Y^2) - \operatorname{E}^2(X) \cdot \operatorname{E}^2(1/Y).
\end{align}</math>

==Normal ratio distributions{{anchor|Normal|Gaussian ratio distributions}}==
{{split section|Normal ratio distributions|reason=Long section about notable concept.|date=March 2021}}

===Uncorrelated central normal ratio===
When {{tmath|X}} and {{tmath|Y}} are independent and have a [[Gaussian distribution]] with zero mean, the form of their ratio distribution is a [[Cauchy distribution]].
This can be derived by setting {{tmath|1= Z=X/Y = \tan \theta}}, then showing that {{tmath|\theta}} has [[circular symmetry]]. For a bivariate uncorrelated Gaussian distribution we have
<math display="block"> \begin{align}
 p(x,y) &= \frac{1}{\sqrt {2 \pi} } \exp{\left(-\tfrac{x^2}{2}\right)} \times \frac{1}{\sqrt {2\pi}}\exp{\left(-\tfrac{y^2}{2}\right)} \\
        &= \frac{1}{2\pi} \exp{\left(-\tfrac{x^2 + y^2}{2}\right)} \\
        &= \frac{1}{2\pi} \exp{\left(-\frac{r^2}{2}\right)},\ \text{for}\ r^2 = x^2 + y^2.
\end{align} </math>

If {{tmath|p(x,y)}} is a function only of {{tmath|r}}, then {{tmath|\theta}} is uniformly distributed on {{tmath| [0, 2\pi]}} with density {{tmath|\textstyle \frac{1}{2\pi} }}, so the problem reduces to finding the probability distribution of {{tmath|Z}} under the mapping
<math display="block"> Z = X/Y = \tan \theta. </math>

We have, by conservation of probability
<math display="block"> p_z(z) \,|dz| = p_\theta(\theta) \,|d\theta|, </math>
and since {{tmath|1= \textstyle \frac{dz}{d\theta} = \frac{1}{\cos^2 \theta} }},
<math display="block"> p_z(z) = \frac{p_\theta(\theta)}{\left|\frac{dz}{d\theta}\right|} = \frac{1}{2\pi}{\cos^2 \theta}. </math>
Setting
<math display="block"> \cos^2 \theta = \frac{1}{1 + (\tan\theta)^2} = \frac{1}{1 + z^2},</math>
we get
<math display="block"> p_z(z) = \frac{1/(2\pi)}{1 + z^2}. </math>
There is a spurious factor of 2 here. Actually, two values of <math> \theta </math> spaced by <math>\pi</math> map onto the same value of {{tmath|z}}, the density is doubled, and the final result is
<math display="block"> p_z(z) = \frac{1/\pi}{1 + z^2 }, \quad -\infty < z < \infty. </math>

When either of the two normal distributions is non-central, then the result for the distribution of the ratio is much more complicated and is given below in the succinct form presented by [[David Hinkley]].{{sfnp|Hinkley|1969}} The trigonometric method for a ratio does, however, extend to radial distributions like bivariate normals or a bivariate {{Student's t-distribution|link=y}}, in which the density depends only on radius {{tmath|1= r =  \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} }}. It does not extend to the ratio of two independent {{Student's t-distribution}}s, which give the Cauchy ratio shown in a section below for one degree of freedom.

===Uncorrelated noncentral normal ratio===

In the absence of correlation ({{tmath|1= \operatorname{cor}(X,Y)=0}}), the [[probability density function]] of the ratio {{tmath|1= Z = X/Y}} of two normal variables <math>X = \mathcal{N}(\mu_X, \sigma_X^2)</math> and <math>Y = \mathcal{N}(\mu_Y, \sigma_Y^2)</math> is given exactly by the following expression, derived in several sources:{{sfnp|Hinkley|1969}}
<math display="block"> p_Z(z) = \frac{e^{-c/2}}{a^2(z) \cdot 2 \pi \sigma_x \sigma_y} \left(\sqrt{2 \pi } \frac{b(z)}{a(z)} \exp \left(\frac{b^2(z)}{2a^2(z)} \right) \mathrm{erf} \left(\frac{b(z)}{\sqrt{2} a(z)} \right) + 2 \right),</math>
where
<math display="block">\begin{align}
a(z) &= \sqrt{\frac{1}{\sigma_x^2} z^2 + \frac{1}{\sigma_y^2}}, \\
b(z) &= \frac{\mu_x }{\sigma_x^2} z + \frac{\mu_y}{\sigma_y^2}, \\
c    &= \frac{\mu_x^2}{\sigma_x^2} + \frac{\mu_y^2}{\sigma_y^2}.
\end{align}</math>

Under several assumptions (usually fulfilled in practical applications), it is possible to derive a highly accurate ''solid approximation'' to the {{abbr|PDF|probability density function}}. Main benefits include reduced formulae complexity, closed-form {{abbr|CDF|cumulative density function}}, simple defined median, and well defined error management. For the sake of simplicity introduce parameters: {{tmath|1= \textstyle p = \frac{\mu_x}{\sqrt{2}\sigma_x} }}, {{tmath|1= \textstyle q =\frac{\mu_y}{\sqrt{2}\sigma_y} }}, and {{tmath|1= \textstyle r = \frac{\mu_x}{\mu_y} }}. Then the so-called solid approximation <math> p_Z^\dagger(z) </math> to the uncorrelated noncentral normal ratio PDF is expressed by equation{{sfnp|Šimon|Ftorek|2022}}
<math display="block"> p_Z^\dagger(z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \frac{p}{\mathrm{erf}[q]} \frac{1}{r} \frac{1+\frac{p^2}{q^2}\frac{z}{r}}{\left(1+\frac{p^2}{q^2}\left[\frac{z}{r}\right]^2\right)^\frac{3}{2}} \exp\left({-\frac{p^2\left(\frac{z}{r}-1 \right)^2}{1+\frac{p^2}{q^2}\left[\frac{z}{r}\right]^2}}\right).</math>

Under certain conditions, a normal approximation is possible, with variance:{{sfnp|Díaz-Francés|Rubio|2012}} <math display="block">\sigma_z^2=\frac{\mu_x^2}{\mu_y^2} \left(\frac{\sigma_x^2}{\mu_x^2} + \frac{\sigma_y^2}{\mu_y^2}\right).</math>

===Correlated central normal ratio===

The above expression becomes more complicated when the variables {{tmath|X}} and {{tmath|Y}} are correlated. If {{tmath|1= \mu_x =}} {{tmath|1= \mu_y = 0}} but {{tmath|\sigma_X \neq \sigma_Y}} and {{tmath|\rho \neq 0}}, the more general Cauchy distribution is obtained,
<math display="block">p_Z(z) = \frac{1}{\pi} \frac{\beta}{(z-\alpha)^2 + \beta^2},</math>
where {{tmath|\rho}} is the [[Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient|correlation coefficient]] between {{tmath|X}} and {{tmath|Y}}, and
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\alpha &= \rho \frac{\sigma_x}{\sigma_y}, \\
\beta  &= \frac{\sigma_x}{\sigma_y} \sqrt{1-\rho^2}.
\end{align}</math>

The complex distribution has also been expressed with Kummer's [[confluent hypergeometric function]] or the [[Hermite function]].{{sfnp|Pham-Gia|Turkkan|Marchand|2006}}

===Correlated noncentral normal ratio===
This was shown in Springer.{{sfnp|Springer|1979|loc=problem 4.28}}

A transformation to the log domain was suggested by Katz{{sfnp|Katz|Baptista|Azen|Pike|1978}} {{See below|{{section link||Binomial distribution}}, below}}. Let the ratio be
<math display="block"> T \sim \frac{\mu_x + \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_x^2 )}{\mu_y + \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_y^2 )}
= \frac{\mu_x + X}{\mu_y + Y}
= \frac{\mu_x}{\mu_y}\frac{1+ \frac{X}{\mu_x}}{1+ \frac{Y}{\mu_y}}. </math>

Take the logarithm of both sides to get
<math display="block"> \ln(T) = \ln \left(\frac{\mu_x}{\mu_y} \right)
 + \ln \left( 1+ \frac{X}{\mu_x} \right)
 - \ln \left( 1+ \frac{Y}{\mu_y} \right).</math>
Observing that {{tmath|1= \ln(1+\delta) = \delta - \frac{\delta^2}{2} + \frac{\delta^3}{3} + \cdots }}, then asymptotically
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\ln(T) &\approx \ln \left(\frac{\mu_x}{\mu_y} \right)+ \frac{X}{\mu_x} - \frac{Y}{\mu_y} \\
  &\sim \ln \left(\frac{\mu_x}{\mu_y} \right) + \mathcal{N} \left( 0, \frac{\sigma_x^2}{\mu_x^2} + \frac{\sigma_y^2}{\mu_y^2} - 2 \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\mu_x \mu_y} \right).
\end{align}</math>

Alternatively, Geary suggested in 1930 that
<math display="block">t \approx \frac{\mu_y T - \mu_x}{\sqrt{\sigma_y^2 T^2 - 2\rho \sigma_x \sigma_y T + \sigma_x^2}}</math>
has approximately a [[Normal Distribution#Definitions|standard Gaussian distribution]];{{sfnp|Geary|1930}} This transformation has been called the ''Geary–Hinkley transformation''.{{sfnp|Hayya|Armstrong|Gressis|1975}} The approximation is good if {{tmath|Y}} is unlikely to assume negative values, i.e., {{tmath|1= \textstyle \mu_y > 3\sigma_y}}.

====Exact correlated noncentral normal ratio====
{{synthesis|section|date=November 2019}}

This is developed by Springer{{sfnp|Springer|1979|loc=problem 4.28}} and Hinkley.{{sfnp|Hinkley|1969}} Geary showed how the correlated ratio {{tmath|z}} could be transformed into a near-Gaussian form and developed an approximation for {{tmath|t}} dependent on the probability of negative denominator values {{tmath|x + \mu_x < 0}} being vanishingly small. Fieller's later correlated ratio analysis is exact but care is needed when combining modern math packages with verbal conditions in the older literature.{{citation needed|date=June 2026}} Pham-Ghia has exhaustively discussed these methods.{{citation needed|date=June 2026}} Hinkley's correlated results are exact but it is shown below that the correlated ratio condition can also be transformed into an uncorrelated one so only the simplified Hinkley equations above are required, not the full correlated ratio version.

Let the ratio be:
<math display="block">z=\frac {x+\mu_x}{y+\mu_y}</math>
in which {{tmath|x, y}} are zero-mean correlated normal variables with variances {{tmath|\sigma_x^2, \sigma_y^2}} and {{tmath|X, Y}} have means {{tmath|\mu_x, \mu_y}}.
Write <math display="inline">x'=x-\rho y\tfrac{\sigma_x}{\sigma_y}</math> such that {{tmath|x', y}} become uncorrelated and {{tmath|x'}} has [[standard deviation]] {{tmath|1= \textstyle \sigma_x' = \sigma_x \sqrt {1- \rho^2} }}. Then the ratio
<math display="block">z = \frac{x' + \rho y\tfrac{\sigma_x}{\sigma_y}+\mu_x}{y+\mu_y}</math>
is invariant under this transformation and retains the same {{abbr|PDF|probability density function}}.

The {{tmath|y}} term in the numerator appears to be made separable by expanding
<math display="block">{x' + \rho y \tfrac{\sigma_x}{\sigma_y} +\mu_x} = x'+\mu_x -\rho \mu_y \tfrac{\sigma_x}{\sigma_y} + \rho (y+\mu_y)\tfrac{\sigma_x}{\sigma_y}</math>
to get
<math display="block">z=\frac {x'+\mu_x'}{y+\mu_y} + \rho \frac{ \sigma_x}{\sigma_y}</math>
in which <math display="inline">\mu'_x=\mu_x - \rho \mu_y \frac { \sigma_x }{\sigma_y} </math> and {{tmath|z}} has now become a ratio of uncorrelated non-central normal samples with an invariant {{tmath|z}}-offset.{{efn|This  is not formally proven, though appears to have been used by Geary}}

Finally, to be explicit, the PDF of the ratio {{tmath|z}} for correlated variables is found by inputting the modified parameters {{tmath|\sigma_x', \mu_x'}}, {{tmath|\sigma_y, \mu_y}} and {{tmath|1= \rho' = 0 }} into the Hinkley equation above which returns the PDF for the correlated ratio with a constant offset {{tmath| \textstyle -\rho\tfrac{\sigma_x}{\sigma_y} }} on {{tmath|z}}.

The figures above show an example of a positively correlated ratio with {{tmath|1= \sigma_x =}} {{tmath|1= \sigma_y = 1}}, {{tmath|1= \mu_x = 0}}, {{tmath|1= \mu_y = 0.5}}, and {{tmath|1= \rho = 0.975}}, in which the shaded wedges represent the increment of area selected by given ratio {{tmath| x/y \in [r, r + \delta] }} which accumulates probability where they overlap the distribution. The theoretical distribution, derived from the equations under discussion combined with Hinkley's equations, is highly consistent with a simulation result using 5,000 samples. In the top figure it is clear that for a ratio {{tmath|1= z = x/y \approx 1}} the wedge has almost bypassed the main distribution mass altogether and this explains the [[Maximum and minimum|local minimum]] in the theoretical PDF {{tmath|p_Z(x/y)}}. Conversely as {{tmath|x/y}} moves either toward or away from one the wedge spans more of the central mass, accumulating a higher probability.

===Complex normal ratio===
The ratio of correlated zero-mean circularly symmetric [[complex normal distribution|complex normal distributed]] variables was determined by Baxley et al.{{sfnp|Baxley|Waldenhorst|Acosta-Marum|2010}} and has since been extended to the nonzero-mean and nonsymmetric case.{{sfnp|Sourisseau|Wu|Zhou|2022}} In the correlated zero-mean case, the joint distribution of {{tmath|x, y}} is
<math display="block"> f_{x,y}(x,y) = \frac{1}{\pi^2 |\Sigma|} \exp \left ( - \begin{bmatrix} x  \\ y  \end{bmatrix}^H \Sigma ^{-1} \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y  \end{bmatrix} \right ) </math>
where
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\Sigma &= \begin{bmatrix}
 \sigma_x^2 & \rho \sigma_x \sigma_y  \\
 \rho^* \sigma_x \sigma_y &  \sigma_y^2  \end{bmatrix}; \\
x &= x_r+ix_i; \\
y &= y_r+iy_i;
\end{align}</math>
<math display="inline">(\cdot)^H </math> is an [[Hermitian transpose]]; and
<math display="block"> \rho = \rho_r +i \rho_i
= \operatorname{E} \bigg(\frac{xy^*}{\sigma_x \sigma_y} \bigg )\; \in \left |\mathbb{C} \right| \le 1.</math>

The {{abbr|PDF|probability density function}} of {{tmath|1= Z = X/Y}} is found to be

<math display="block">\begin{align}
 f_{z}(z_r,z_i) & = \frac{1-|\rho|^2}{\pi \sigma_x^2 \sigma_y^2 }
 \left( \frac{|z|^2}{\sigma_x^2} + \frac{1}{\sigma_y^2} -2\frac{\rho_r z_r - \rho_i z_i}{\sigma_x \sigma_y} \right)^{-2} \\[1ex]
& = \frac{1-|\rho|^2}{\pi \sigma_x^2 \sigma_y^2 }
\left( \left| \frac{z}{\sigma_x} - \frac{\rho^* }{\sigma_y} \right|^2 + \frac{1-|\rho|^2}{\sigma_y^2} \right)^{-2}.
\end{align} </math>
In the usual event that <math> \sigma_x = \sigma_y </math> we get
<math display="block">f_{z}(z_r,z_i) = \frac{1 - \left|\rho\right|^2}{\pi \left(\left|z - \rho^* \right|^2 + 1 - \left|\rho\right|^2 \right)^2}.</math>

Further closed-form results for the {{abbr|CDF|cumulative distribution function}} are also given.

[[File:cmplxratio.jpg|thumb|The ratio distribution of correlated complex variables, {{math|1=''ρ'' = 0.7 ''e''{{sup|''iπ''/4}}}}.]]

The graph shows the pdf of the ratio of two complex normal variables with a correlation coefficient of {{tmath|1= \textstyle \rho = 0.7 e^{i\pi/4} }}. The PDF peak occurs at roughly the [[complex conjugate]] of a scaled down {{tmath|\rho}}.

== Ratio of log-normal ==

The ratio of independent or correlated log-normals is log-normal.  This follows, because if <math>X_1</math> and <math>X_2</math> are [[log-normal distribution|log-normally distributed]], then <math>\ln(X_1)</math> and <math>\ln(X_2)</math> are normally distributed.  If they are independent or their logarithms follow a [[multivariate normal#Bivariate case|bivarate normal distribution]], then the [[logarithm]] of their ratio is the difference of independent or correlated normally distributed random variables, which is normally distributed.{{efn|Note, however, that <math>X_1</math> and <math>X_2</math> can be individually [[log-normal distribution|log-normally distributed]] without having a bivariate log-normal distribution. {{Crossreference|{{As of|2022|06|08}} the [[Copula (probability theory)]] article includes a density and contour plot of two Normal marginals joint with a Gumbel copula, where the joint distribution is not bivariate normal.}}}}

This is important for many applications requiring the ratio of random variables that must be positive, where joint distribution of <math>X_1</math> and <math>X_2</math> is adequately approximated by a log-normal.  This is a common result of the [[log-normal#Multiplicative Central Limit Theorem|multiplicative central limit theorem]], also known as [[Gibrat's law]], when <math>X_i</math> is the result of an accumulation of many small percentage changes and must be positive and approximately log-normally distributed.{{efn|Of course, any invocation of a [[central limit theorem]] assumes suitable, commonly met regularity conditions, e.g., finite variance.}}

==Uniform ratio distribution==
With two independent random variables following a [[uniform distribution (continuous)|uniform distribution]], e.g.,
<math display="block">p_X(x) = \begin{cases}
1, & 0 < x < 1 \\
0, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}</math>
the ratio distribution becomes
<math display="block">p_Z(z) = \begin{cases}
\tfrac{1}{2},     & 0 < z < 1 \\
\tfrac{1}{2z^2},  & z \geq 1  \\
0,                & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}</math>

==Cauchy ratio distribution==
If two independent random variables, {{tmath|X}} and {{tmath|Y}} each follow a [[Cauchy distribution]] with median equal to zero and shape factor {{tmath|a}},
<math display="block">p_X(x|a) = \frac{a}{\pi (a^2 + x^2)},</math>
then the ratio distribution for the random variable {{tmath|1= Z = X/Y}} is{{sfnp|Kermond|2010}}
<math display="block">p_Z(z|a) = \frac{1}{\pi^2(z^2-1)} \ln(z^2).</math>
This distribution does not depend on {{tmath|a}} and the result stated by Springer{{sfnp|Springer|1979|p=158|loc=Question 4.6}} is not correct.

The ratio distribution is similar to but not the same as the [[product distribution]] of the random variable {{tmath|1= W = XY}}:{{sfnp|Springer|1979}}
<math display="block">p_W(w|a) = \frac{a^2}{\pi^2(w^2-a^4)} \ln \left(\frac{w^2}{a^4}\right).</math>

More generally, if two independent random variables {{tmath|X}} and {{tmath|Y}} each follow a [[Cauchy distribution]] with median equal to zero and shape factor {{tmath|a}} and {{tmath|b}} respectively, then:
# The ratio distribution for the random variable {{tmath|1= Z = X/Y}} is{{sfnp|Kermond|2010}} <math display="block">p_Z(z|a,b) = \frac{ab}{\pi^2(b^2z^2-a^2)} \ln \left(\frac{b^2 z^2}{a^2}\right).</math>
# The [[product distribution]] for the random variable {{tmath|1= W = XY}} is{{sfnp|Kermond|2010}} <math display="block">p_W(w|a,b) = \frac{ab}{\pi^2(w^2-a^2b^2)} \ln \left(\frac{w^2}{a^2b^2}\right).</math>
The result for the ratio distribution can be obtained from the product distribution by replacing {{tmath|b}} with {{tmath|\textstyle \tfrac{1}{b} }}.

==Ratio of standard normal to standard uniform==
{{main|Slash distribution}}
If {{tmath|X}} has a standard normal distribution and {{tmath|Y}} has a standard uniform distribution, then {{tmath|1= Z = X/Y}} has a distribution known as the ''[[slash distribution]]'', with probability density function
<math display="block">p_Z(z) = \begin{cases}
\frac{\left[ \varphi(0) - \varphi(z) \right]}{z^2}, &  z \ne 0 \\
\frac{\varphi(0)}{2}, & z = 0, \\
\end{cases}</math>
where {{tmath|\varphi(z)}} is the probability density function of the standard normal distribution.<ref name="nist">{{cite web |date=2004 |title=SLAPPF |url=http://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/software/dataplot/refman2/auxillar/slappf.htm |access-date=2009-07-02 |publisher=Statistical Engineering Division, National Institute of Science and Technology}}</ref>

==Chi-squared, Gamma distributions==

Let {{tmath|G}} be a normal distribution {{tmath|\mathcal(0,1)}}, {{tmath|Y}} and {{tmath|Z}} be [[chi-squared distribution]]s with {{tmath|m}} and {{tmath|n}} [[degrees of freedom]] respectively, all independent, with
<math display="block">f_\chi(x,k) = \frac{x^{\left(\tfrac{k}{2}-1\right)}e^{-\tfrac{x}{2}} }{2^{k/2}\Gamma\left(\tfrac{k}{2}\right)}.</math> 
Then
* <math display="inline"> \frac{ G }{ \sqrt{ Y / m } } \sim t_m </math> is the {{Student's t-distribution|link=y}};
* <math display="inline"> \frac{ Y / m }{ Z / n }  = F_{ m, n }, </math> i.e. Fisher's [[F-test|{{italics correction|''F''}}-test]] distribution;
* <math display="inline"> \frac{ Y }{ Y + Z } \sim \beta( \tfrac{m}{2},\tfrac{n}{2} )</math> is the [[beta distribution]]; and 
* <math display="inline"> \frac{ Y }{ Z } \sim \beta'( \tfrac{m}{2},\tfrac{n}{2} )</math> is the ''standard'' [[beta prime distribution]].

If {{tmath|1= \textstyle V_1 \sim {\chi'}_{k_1}^2(\lambda) }}, a [[noncentral chi-squared distribution]], {{tmath|1= \textstyle V_2 \sim {\chi'}_{k_2}^2(0) }}, and {{tmath|V_1}} is independent of {{tmath|V_2}}, then
<math display="block">\frac{V_1/k_1}{V_2/k_2} \sim F'_{k_1,k_2}(\lambda),</math> a [[noncentral F-distribution|noncentral {{italics correction|''F''}}F-distribution]].

<math display="inline">\tfrac{m}{n} F'_{m,n} = \beta'( \tfrac{m}{2},\tfrac{n}{2})</math> or <math>F'_{m,n} = \beta'( \tfrac{m}{2},\tfrac{n}{2} ,1,\tfrac{n }{m})</math> 
defines {{tmath| F'_{m,n} }}, Fisher's {{italics correction|''F''}} density distribution, the {{abbr|PDF|probability density function}} of the ratio of two [[chi-squared distribution]]s with {{tmath|m, n}} degrees of freedom.{{efn|{{crossreference|The {{abbr|CDF|cumulative distribution function}} of the Fisher density, found in {{italics correction|''F''}}-tables is defined in [[beta prime distribution]].}}}}

If we enter an {{italics correction|''F''}}-test table with {{tmath|1= m=3 }}, {{tmath|1= n=4 }} and 5% probability in the right tail, the critical value is found to be 6.59.  This coincides with the integral
<math display="block"> F_{3,4}(6.59) = \int_{6.59}^\infty \beta'(x; \tfrac{m}{2},\tfrac{n}{2},1,\tfrac{n}{m} ) \,  dx = 0.05 .</math>

For [[gamma distribution]]s {{tmath|U}} and {{tmath|V}} with arbitrary [[Gamma distribution#Characterization using shape k and scale θ|shape parameters]] {{tmath|\alpha_1}} and {{tmath|\alpha_2}}, and their scale parameters both set to unity (that is, {{tmath|1= \textstyle U \sim \Gamma (\alpha_1, 1)}}, {{tmath|1= \textstyle V \sim \Gamma(\alpha_2, 1)}}, where {{tmath|1= \textstyle \Gamma(x;\alpha,1) = (x^{\alpha-1}e^{-x})/{\Gamma(\alpha)} }}), then

<math display="block">\begin{align}
 \tfrac{U}{U+V} &\sim \beta(\alpha_1, \alpha_2), & \text{ expectation } &= \tfrac{\alpha_1}{\alpha_1 + \alpha_2 }; \\[1ex]
 \tfrac{U}{V} & \sim \beta'(\alpha_1, \alpha_2), & \text{ expectation } &= \tfrac{\alpha_1}{ \alpha_2 -1},\; \alpha_2 > 1; \\[1ex]
 \tfrac{V}{U} & \sim \beta'(\alpha_2, \alpha_1), & \text{ expectation } &= \tfrac{\alpha_2}{ \alpha_1 -1},\; \alpha_1 > 1.
\end{align}</math>

If {{tmath|1= U \sim \Gamma(x;\alpha,1) }}, then
<math display="block">\theta U \sim \Gamma (x;\alpha,\theta) = \frac { x^{\alpha-1} e^{- x/\theta}}{  \theta^k \Gamma(\alpha)}.</math>
Note that here {{tmath|\theta}} is a [[Gamma distribution#Characterization using shape k and scale θ|scale parameter]], rather than a rate parameter.

If  {{tmath|1= U \sim \Gamma(\alpha_1,\theta_1)}}, {{tmath|1= V \sim\Gamma(\alpha_2,\theta_2)}}, then by rescaling the {{tmath|\theta}} parameter to unity we have
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\frac {\frac {U}{\theta_1}} {\frac {U}{\theta_1} + \frac {V}{\theta_2}}
&= \frac{ \theta_2 U }{ \theta_2 U + \theta_1 V } \sim \beta( \alpha_1, \alpha_2 ) \\
\frac {\frac {U}{\theta_1}} {\frac {V}{\theta_2}}
& = \frac{ \theta_2 }{ \theta_1  } \frac{U }{ V }\sim \beta'( \alpha_1, \alpha_2 ).
\end{align}</math>
Thus
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\frac{U}{V} &\sim \beta'\left(\alpha_1, \alpha_2, 1, \frac{\theta_1}{\theta_2} \right) \\
\operatorname{E} \left[\frac{U}{V}\right] &= \frac{\theta_1}{\theta_2} \frac{\alpha_1}{\alpha_2 - 1},
\end{align}</math>
in which <math>\beta'(\alpha,\beta,p,q)</math> represents the [[Beta prime distribution#Generalization|''generalised'' beta prime distribution]].

In the foregoing it is apparent that if <math> X \sim \beta'( \alpha_1, \alpha_2, 1, 1 ) \equiv \beta'( \alpha_1, \alpha_2 ) </math> then <math> \theta X \sim \beta'( \alpha_1, \alpha_2, 1, \theta ) </math>.  More explicitly, since
<math display="block">  \beta'(x; \alpha_1, \alpha_2, 1, R ) = \frac{1}{R} \beta' (\frac{x}{R} ; \alpha_1, \alpha_2) </math>
if <math> U \sim \Gamma(\alpha_1, \theta_1 ), V \sim \Gamma(\alpha_2, \theta_2 ) </math>
then
<math display="block"> \frac {U}{V} \sim \frac{1}{R}  \beta' ( \frac{x}{R}  ; \alpha_1, \alpha_2 )
= \frac { \left(\frac{x}{R} \right)^{\alpha_1-1} } {\left(1+\frac{x}{R} \right)^{\alpha_1+\alpha_2}} \cdot
 \frac {1} { \;R\;B( \alpha_1, \alpha_2 )},</math>
where
<math display="block">\begin{align}
x &\ge 0; \\
R &= \frac {\theta_1}{\theta_2}; \\
B(\alpha_1, \alpha_2) &=  \frac{\Gamma(\alpha_1)\Gamma(\alpha_2)}{\Gamma(\alpha_1 + \alpha_2)}.
\end{align}</math>

==Beta distributions==

First developed by T. Pham-Gia{{sfnp|Pham-Gia|2000}} who found that the PDF of a Beta ratio can be expressed in terms of hypergeometric functions.  These are calculated numerically as an infinite discrete sum or as an integral. The latter is straightforward such that, if <math> Y </math> is the ratio of two independent Beta samples <math> Y = X_1/X_2 </math>, each with PDF <math> B(\alpha, \beta)^{-1} x^{\alpha-1} (1-x)^{\beta-1} </math> proceeds in two ranges <math> 0 \le y <  1 </math> and <math> 1 < y < \infty\, </math>  thus

<math display="block"> \begin{align}
&f_A(y|0 < y \le 1) = \frac{1}{B(\alpha_1,\beta_1)(\alpha_2,\beta_2)} y^{\alpha_1 - 1}
 \int_0^1 dp \; p^{\alpha1+\alpha_2 -1 } 
(1 - p)^{\beta_2 -1} ( 1- py)^{\beta_1-1} \\[6pt]

& f_B(y|1< y<\infty) = \frac{1}{B(\alpha_1,\beta_1)(\alpha_2,\beta_2)} \frac{1}{y^{\alpha_2 + 1}}
 \int_0^1 dp \; p^{\alpha1+\alpha_2 -1 } 
(1 - p)^{\beta_1-1} \left ( 1- \frac{y}{p} \right)^{\beta_2-1} 
\end{align}  </math>

==Rayleigh Distributions==

If  ''X'', ''Y'' are independent samples from the [[Rayleigh distribution]] <math> f_r(r) = (r/\sigma^2) e^ {-r^2/2\sigma^2}, \;\; r \ge 0 </math>, the ratio ''Z'' = ''X''/''Y'' follows the distribution{{sfnp|Hamedani|2013}}

<math display="block"> f_z(z) = \frac{2  z}{ (1 +  z^2 )^2 }, \;\; z \ge 0 </math>
and has cdf
<math display="block"> F_z(z) = 1 - \frac{1}{ 1 + z^2 } = \frac{z^2}{ 1 + z^2 }, \;\;\; z \ge 0  </math>
The Rayleigh distribution has scaling as its only parameter.  The distribution of <math> Z = \alpha X/Y </math> follows
<math display="block"> f_z(z,\alpha) = \frac{2 \alpha z}{ (\alpha +  z^2 )^2 }, \;\; z > 0 </math>
and has cdf
<math display="block"> F_z(z, \alpha) = \frac{ z^2 }{ \alpha + z^2 }, \;\;\; z \ge 0  </math>

== Fractional gamma distributions (including chi, chi-squared, exponential, Rayleigh and Weibull) ==

The [[generalized gamma distribution]] is
<math display="block"> f(x;a,d,r)=\frac{r}{\Gamma(d/r) a^d } x^{d-1} e^{-(x/a)^r} \; x \ge 0; \;\; a, \; d, \;r > 0</math>
which includes the regular gamma, chi, chi-squared, exponential, Rayleigh, Nakagami and Weibull distributions involving fractional powers.  Note that here ''a'' is a [[Gamma distribution#Characterization using shape k and scale θ|scale parameter]], rather than a rate parameter;  ''d'' is a shape parameter.

{{block indent | em = 1.5 | text =
If <math> U \sim f(x;a_1,d_1,r), \; \; V \sim f(x;a_2,d_2,r) \text{ are independent, and  } W = U/V </math>
then{{sfnp|Rao|Garg|1969}} <math display="inline"> g(w) = \frac{r \left ( \frac {a_1}{a_2} \right )^{d_2}   }{B \left ( \frac{d_1}{r}, \frac{d_2}{r} \right ) } \frac{w^{-d_2 -1}}{ \left( 1 + \left( \frac{a_2}{a_1} \right)^{-r} w^{-r} \right) ^ \frac{d_1+d_2}{r} } ,  \; \; w>0 </math>
where {{tmath|1= B(u,v) = \frac{\Gamma(u) \Gamma(v)}{\Gamma(u+v)} }}.}}

===Modelling a mixture of different scaling factors===

In the ratios above, Gamma samples, '''''U''''', '''''V''''' may have differing sample sizes <math> \alpha_1, \alpha_2 </math> but must be drawn from the same distribution <math>  \frac { x^{\alpha-1} e^{-x/\theta}}{  \theta^k \Gamma(\alpha)} </math> with equal scaling <math>\theta</math>.

In situations where '''''U''''' and '''''V''''' are differently scaled, a variables transformation allows the modified random ratio pdf to be determined. Let <math> X = \frac {U} { U + V} = \frac {1} { 1 + B} </math> where <math> U \sim \Gamma(\alpha_1,\theta), V \sim \Gamma(\alpha_2,\theta), \theta </math> arbitrary and, from above, <math> X \sim \mathrm{Beta}(\alpha_1, \alpha_2), B = V/U \sim \mathrm{Beta}'(\alpha_2, \alpha_1) </math>.

Rescale '''''V''''' arbitrarily, defining <math> Y \sim \frac {U} { U + \varphi V} = \frac {1} { 1 + \varphi B}, \;\; 0 \le \varphi \le \infty </math>

We have <math> B = \frac{1-X}{X}  </math> and substitution into '''''Y''''' gives <math> Y = \frac {X}{\varphi + (1-\varphi)X} </math>, <math>dY/dX = \frac {\varphi}{(\varphi + (1-\varphi)X)^2}</math>

Transforming '''''X''''' to '''''Y''''' gives <math> f_Y(Y) = \frac{f_X (X) } {| dY/dX|} = \frac {\beta(X,\alpha_1,\alpha_2)}{ \varphi / [\varphi + (1-\varphi) X]^2} </math>

Noting <math> X = \frac {\varphi Y}{ 1-(1 - \varphi)Y} </math>  we finally have
<math display="block"> f_Y(Y, \varphi) = \frac{\varphi } { [1 - (1 - \varphi)Y]^2} \beta{\left (\frac {\varphi Y}{ 1 - (1-\varphi) Y}, \alpha_1, \alpha_2 \right)}, \;\;\; 0 \le Y \le 1 </math>

Thus, if <math> U \sim \Gamma(\alpha_1,\theta_1) </math> and <math> V \sim \Gamma(\alpha_2,\theta_2)  </math>
<br>then <math> Y = \frac {U} { U + V} </math> is distributed as <math> f_Y(Y, \varphi) </math> with <math> \varphi = \frac {\theta_2}{\theta_1} </math>

The distribution of '''''Y''''' is limited here to the interval [0,1].  It can be generalized by scaling such that if <math> Y \sim f_Y(Y,\varphi)  </math>  then

<math display="block"> \Theta Y \sim   f_Y( Y,\varphi, \Theta)  </math>

where <math> f_Y( Y,\varphi, \Theta) = \frac{\varphi / \Theta } { [1 - (1 - \varphi)Y / \Theta]^2} \beta \left (\frac {\varphi Y / \Theta}{ 1 - (1-\varphi) Y / \Theta}, \alpha_1, \alpha_2 \right), \;\;\; 0 \le Y \le \Theta </math>
{{block indent | em = 1.5 | text = <math> \Theta Y </math> is then a sample from <math> \frac {\Theta U} { U + \varphi V}  </math>}}

==Reciprocals of samples from beta distributions==

Though not ratio distributions of two variables, the following identities for one variable are useful:

* If <math>X \sim \beta (\alpha,\beta)</math> then <math> \mathbf x = \frac{X}{1-X} \sim \beta'(\alpha,\beta) </math>
* If <math> \mathbf Y \sim \beta' (\alpha,\beta)</math> then <math> y = \frac{1}{\mathbf Y} \sim \beta'(\beta,\alpha) </math> combining the latter two equations yields
* If <math>X \sim \beta (\alpha,\beta)</math> then <math> \mathbf x = \frac{1}{X} -1 \sim \beta'(\beta,\alpha) </math>.
* If <math> \mathbf Y \sim \beta' (\alpha,\beta)</math> then <math> y = \frac{\mathbf Y}{1 + \mathbf Y} \sim \beta(\alpha,\beta) </math>
Corollary

<math display="block"> \frac{1}{1 + \mathbf Y}
 =  \frac{ \mathbf Y ^ {-1}}{\mathbf Y^{-1} + 1} \sim \beta(\beta,\alpha) </math>

{{block indent | em = 1.5 | text = <math> 1 + \mathbf Y \sim \{ \; \beta(\beta,\alpha) \; \} ^{-1}  </math>,  the distribution of the reciprocals of <math> \beta(\beta,\alpha) </math>  samples.}}
If <math> U \sim \Gamma ( \alpha , 1), V \sim \Gamma(\beta, 1) </math> then <math> \frac{U}{V} \sim \beta' ( \alpha, \beta )</math> and
<math display="block">\frac{U / V}{1+U / V} = \frac{U}{V + U } \sim \beta(\alpha,\beta) </math>

Further results can be found in the [[Inverse distribution]] article.

* If {{mvar|X}}, {{mvar|Y}} are independent exponential random variables with mean {{mvar|μ}}, then {{math|''X'' − ''Y''}} is a [[Laplace distribution|double exponential]] random variable with mean 0 and scale {{mvar|μ}}.

==Binomial distribution==

This result was derived by Katz et al.{{sfnp|Katz|Baptista|Azen|Pike|1978}}

Suppose <math>X \sim \operatorname{Binomial}(n,p_1)</math> and <math>Y \sim \text{Binomial}(m,p_2)</math> and {{tmath|X}}, <math>Y</math> are independent. Let {{tmath|1= T = \frac{X/n}{Y/m} }}.

Then <math>\log(T)</math> is approximately normally distributed with mean <math>\log(p_1/p_2)</math> and variance {{tmath|\frac{(1/p_1)-1}{n} + \frac{(1/p_2)-1}{m} }}.

The binomial ratio distribution is of significance in clinical trials: if the distribution of ''T'' is known as above, the probability of a given ratio arising purely by chance can be estimated, i.e. a false positive trial.  A number of papers compare the robustness of different approximations for the binomial ratio.{{citation needed|date=November 2019}}

==Poisson and truncated Poisson distributions==

In the ratio of Poisson variables {{math|1= ''R'' = ''X''/''Y''}} there is a problem that {{mvar|Y}} is zero with finite probability so {{mvar|R}} is undefined. To counter this,  consider the truncated, or censored, ratio {{math|1= ''{{prime|R}}'' = ''X''/''Y''}} where zero sample of {{mvar|Y}} are discounted.  Moreover, in many medical-type surveys, there are systematic problems with the reliability of the zero samples of both {{mvar|X}} and {{mvar|Y}} and it may be good practice to ignore the zero samples anyway.

The probability of a null Poisson sample being {{tmath|e^{-\lambda} }}, the generic {{abbr|PDF|probability density function}} of a left truncated Poisson distribution is
<math display="block"> \tilde p_x(x;\lambda)= \frac {1}{1-e^{-\lambda} }
{ \frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^{x}}{x!} }, \;\;\; x \in 1,2,3, \cdots </math>
which sums to unity. Following Cohen,{{sfnp|Cohen|1960}} for {{mvar|n}} independent trials, the multidimensional truncated {{abbr|PDF|probability density function}} is
<math display="block"> \tilde p(x_1, x_2, \dots ,x_n;\lambda)= \frac{1}{\left(1-e^{-\lambda}\right)^n }
\prod_{i=1}^n{ \frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^{x_i}}{x_i!} }, \;\;\; x_i \in 1,2,3, \cdots
 </math>
and the log-likelihood becomes
<math display="block"> L = \ln (\tilde p) = - n \ln \left(1 - e^{-\lambda}\right)
- n \lambda + \ln(\lambda) \sum_{i=1}^n x_i  - \ln \prod_{i=1}^n (x_i!), \;\;\; x_i \in 1,2,3, \cdots
 </math>
On differentiation we get
<math display="block"> \frac{dL}{d\lambda}  = \frac{-n}{ 1-e^{-\lambda}} + \frac{1}{\lambda}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i    </math>
and setting to zero gives the maximum likelihood estimate <math> \hat \lambda_\text{ML} </math>
<math display="block"> \frac{\hat \lambda_\text{ML}}{ 1-e^{-\hat \lambda_\text{ML} }} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n x_i = \bar x </math>

Note that as <math> \hat \lambda \to 0 </math> then <math> \bar x \to 1 </math> so the truncated maximum likelihood <math> \lambda </math> estimate, though correct for both truncated and untruncated distributions, gives a [[truncated mean]] <math> \bar x </math> value which is highly biassed relative to the untruncated one. Nevertheless it appears that <math> \bar x </math> is a [[sufficient statistic]] for <math> \lambda </math> since <math> \hat \lambda_{ML} </math> depends on the data only through the sample mean <math>  \bar x = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n x_i  </math> in the previous equation which is consistent with the methodology of the conventional [[Poisson distribution]].

Absent any closed form solutions, the following approximate reversion for truncated <math> \lambda </math> is valid over the whole range {{tmath| 0 \le \lambda \le \infty; \; 1 \le \bar x \le \infty }}.
<math display="block"> \hat \lambda = \bar x - e^{-( \bar x -1) } - 0.07(\bar x -1)e^{-0.666(\bar x-1)}  + \varepsilon, \;\;\;|\varepsilon | < 0.006  </math>
which compares with the non-truncated version which is simply <math> \hat \lambda = \bar x  </math>.  Taking the ratio <math> R = \hat \lambda_X / \hat \lambda_Y </math> is a valid operation even though <math>  \hat \lambda_X  </math> may use a non-truncated model while <math>  \hat \lambda_Y  </math> has a left-truncated one.

The asymptotic large-<math>  n\lambda  </math> variance of <math>\hat\lambda</math> (and [[Cramér–Rao bound]]) is
<math display="block"> \mathbb{Var} ( \hat \lambda ) \ge - \left( \mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{\delta ^2 L }{ \delta \lambda^2 } \right]_{\lambda=\hat \lambda} \right) ^{-1}  </math>

in which substituting {{mvar|L}} gives
<math display="block"> \frac{\delta ^2 L }{ \delta \lambda^2 } =
-n \left[ \frac{ \bar x}{\lambda ^2 } -  \frac{e^{-\lambda}}{(1-e^{-\lambda})^2  } \right] </math>
Then substituting <math> \bar x </math> from the equation above, we get Cohen's variance estimate
<math display="block"> \mathbb{Var} ( \hat \lambda )  \ge \frac{ \hat\lambda}{n}  \frac { (1-e^{-\hat\lambda})^2 }{ 1 - (\hat\lambda + 1) e^{-\hat\lambda} }  </math>

The variance of the point estimate of the mean {{tmath|\lambda}}, on the basis of {{mvar|n}} trials, decreases asymptotically to zero as {{mvar|n}} increases to infinity. For small <math> \lambda </math> it diverges from the truncated pdf variance in Springael{{sfnp|Springael|2006}} for example, who quotes a variance of
<math display="block"> \mathbb {Var} ( \lambda) = \frac {\lambda / n}{1-e^{-\lambda}} \left [ 1 - \frac{\lambda e^{-\lambda} }{1-e^{-\lambda}}\right]  </math>
for ''n'' samples in the left-truncated pdf shown at the top of this section.  Cohen showed that the variance of the estimate relative to the variance of the pdf, <math> \mathbb {Var} ( \hat \lambda) / \mathbb {Var} ( \lambda) </math>, ranges from 1 for large <math>  \lambda </math> (100% efficient) up to 2 as <math>  \lambda </math> approaches zero (50% efficient).

These mean and variance parameter estimates, together with parallel estimates for ''X'', can be applied to Normal or Binomial approximations for the Poisson ratio.  Samples from trials may not be a good fit for the Poisson process; a further discussion of Poisson truncation is by Dietz and Bohning{{sfnp|Dietz|Bohning|2000}} and there is a [[Zero-truncated Poisson distribution]] Wikipedia entry.

==Double Lomax distribution==

This distribution is the ratio of two [[Laplace distribution]]s.{{sfnp|Bindu|Sangita|2015}} Let ''X'' and ''Y'' be standard Laplace identically distributed random variables and let ''z'' = ''X'' / ''Y''. Then the probability distribution of ''z'' is

<math display="block"> f( x ) = \frac{ 1 }{ 2 \left( 1 + |z| \right)^2 } </math>

Let the mean of the ''X'' and ''Y'' be ''a''. Then the standard double [[Lomax distribution]] is symmetric around ''a''.

This distribution has an infinite mean and variance.

If ''Z'' has a standard double Lomax distribution, then 1/''Z'' also has a standard double Lomax distribution.

The standard Lomax distribution is unimodal and has heavier tails than the Laplace distribution.

For 0 < ''a'' < 1, the ''a''-th moment exists.

<math display="block">\Lambda = \frac{|\mathbf{X}|}{|\mathbf{X}+\mathbf{Y}|} </math><math display="block"> E( Z^a ) = \frac{ \Gamma( 1 + a ) }{ \Gamma( 1 - a ) } </math>

where {{math|Γ}} is the [[gamma function]].

== Ratio distributions in multivariate analysis ==
Ratio distributions also appear in [[multivariate analysis]].{{sfnp|Brennan|Reed|1982}} If the random matrices {{math|'''X'''}} and {{math|'''Y'''}} follow a [[Wishart distribution]] then the ratio of the [[determinant]]s
<math display="block">\varphi = \frac{|\mathbf{X}|}{|\mathbf{Y}|}</math>
is proportional to the product of independent [[F-distribution|F]] random variables. In the case where {{math|'''X'''}} and {{math|'''Y'''}} are from independent standardized [[Wishart distribution]]s then the ratio
<math display="block">\Lambda = \frac{|\mathbf{X}|}{|\mathbf{X}+\mathbf{Y}|} </math>
has a [[Wilks' lambda distribution]].

===Ratios of quadratic forms involving Wishart matrices===
In relation to Wishart matrix distributions, if <math> S \sim W_p(\Sigma, \nu + 1)</math> is a sample Wishart matrix, and vector <math> V </math> is arbitrary, but statistically independent, then corollary 3.2.9 of Muirhead{{sfnp|Muirhead|1982|loc=corollary 3.2.9}} states
<math display="block"> \frac{V^T S V}{V^T \Sigma V} \sim \chi^2_\nu. </math>

The discrepancy of one in the sample numbers arises from estimation of the sample mean when forming the sample covariance, a consequence of [[Cochran's theorem]]. Similarly,
<math display="block"> \frac{V^T \Sigma^{-1} V}{V^T S^{-1} V} \sim \chi^2_{\nu-p+1},</math>
which is Theorem 3.2.12 of Muirhead.{{sfnp|Muirhead|1982|p=96|loc=Theorem 3.2.12}}
